newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia's post-war parliament convenes after delay.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia's post-war parliament convenes after delay.

text.p: Bosnian Moslem, Croat and Serb politicians opened the first full session of the country's post-war parliament on Friday, pledging to work for a lasting peace.

The 42-member House of Representatives, elected in September, convened along a former front line in a small room of Sarajevo's National Museum which once housed natural history exhibits of aquariums and snakes.
Former enemies sat uncomfortably close to one another along an aisle and listened to speeches from all three members of the collective presidency led by Alija Izetbegovic, a Moslem.
The parliament session was expected to clear the way for the formation of a peacetime government by approving cabinet nominations submitted by the three-member presidency.
"Now the real work must start," Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative overseeing reconstruction in Bosnia, told the deputies in a speech.
Bosnia's voters "expect you to get the country back on track. They expect you to provide them with peaceful, decent living conditons," the German diplomat said.
Izetbegovic wished the parliament success and called for the deputies to fullly implement the Dayton peace accords which ended the 3-1/2 year war in November 1995.
The Bosnian Serb member of the presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, was greeted with an awkward silence from Moslem and Croat deputies when he rose to deliver his address.

"I can see the SDA (the main Moslem party) is applauding weakly," said Krajisnik, known for his ultra-nationalist beliefs. His speech appeared to cast doubt on Bosnia's sovereignty as a single state, as prescribed by Dayton.

Krajisnik, who bitterly opposed Bosnia's Moslem- and Croat-led secession from old federal Yugoslavia, said the former warring factions had agreed to recognise Bosnia's Moslem-Croat and Serb territories as "two states".
But he also said Bosnia-Herzegovina "exists too".
Saying it was time to heal the wounds of war, Krajisnik warned that the peace would hold only if all three national communities had equal rights.
"Bosnia-Herzegovina can survive if we work hard to ensure all three nations and both entities feel equal and secure."

If all goes as planned, parliament will approve the cabinet known as the Council of Ministers. The council is a weak central government ruling Bosnia's autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories carved out in war.
The parliament later took a recess at midday to allow Moslem deputes to attend Islamic prayers.
Serb deputies had boycotted an inaugural session of parliament in October, snubbing foreign dignitaries who had flown in for the ceremony.
The Serbs had cited objections to the venue in the city centre, which is under Moslem-Croat federation rule, and to the text of an oath pledging loyalty to Bosnia as a single state.
Since then all the Serb deputies have signed the "solemn declaration" to the Bosnian constitution but avoided taking the oath in a public ceremony, diplomats said.

Serb nationalist leaders have suceeded in persuading their Moslem and Croat rivals to accept a temporary arrangement in which the venue for government meetings alternates between the country's Serb republic and Moslem-Croat federation.
A 15-member upper chamber, the House of Peoples, was also due to convene for the first time in the Sarajevo suburb of Lukavica in Serb-controlled territory later on Friday.
